transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marta Alvarez (Stormbridge CTO), Samir Gupta (Stormbridge ML Eng), Ellen Zhou (Stormbridge Infra)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Demo focused on migration parity from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API.
- Discussed API differences (function-calls, streaming, embeddings), dedicated vs hosted, private/VPC deployment, and security (SOC2, KMS, SAML).
- Agreed to a short benchmark pilot and parity spreadsheet share, plus a security scoping call.

Topics: parity mapping, streaming & function calling, latency vs cost tradeoffs, dedicated vs private deploy, KV cache/quantization, audit logs and SSO, pilot checklist

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, um, I'm Jordan Lee, AE at Redwood, with Priya who's our systems and performance SE. Quick agenda: we'll run a short parity walkthrough showing equivalence for the APIs you use today with OpenAI/Anthropic/Together, then demo the Console + Optimize suggestions, and finish with next steps and pilot scoping. Sound good?

[00:12] Marta Alvarez: Yep, that works. Thanks. We wanted to focus on cost parity and streaming behavior esp for our chat product.

[00:18] Samir Gupta: Also function calling, we use a lot of structured outputs for our agents. And latency tail is a concern — p95 under 400ms in prod.

[00:27] Priya Kapoor: Great, we'll show typical request/response mapping. Quick note: Redwood supports streaming, tool / function-calling patterns similar to OpenAI's approach, and has extra knobs for batching, KV cache reuse, and quantization profiles that help cost.

[02:03] Jordan: Quick housekeeping — I'll drop a parity spreadsheet link in the chat at the end, it's got endpoint mappings, parameter equivalents, and a sample changeset for Node/Python.

[03:10] Ellen Zhou: On security, two asks up front: we need audit trail exports and KMS integration. Is that straightforward?

[03:35] Priya: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, and audit logs can be exported to S3 or pushed to your SIEM. We have SOC 2 Type II and some customers pull logs into Splunk for retention. We'll capture details in the next steps.

[04:02] Speaker 1 (Samir or Marta, misc attribution errors): Okay cool.

[04:25] Jordan: Alright demo time — I'm switching to the Console. So on the API parity sheet we map your existing OpenAI call: model=gpt-4-x, max_tokens, temperature, messages => Redwood model names and params. One thing to note: together/together.ai models often have slightly different tokenization; we include tokenization equivalence and suggested prompt substrings to preserve context window.

[06:00] Priya: On function calling — Redwood has the same pattern: declare schema, call returns a structured result. There's also an optional strict schema mode for production where we validate outputs server-side. A lot of customers like that for 3rd-party tool safety.

[07:12] Samir: Is there a gap with Anthropic's approach to safety or token-level controls? We push a lot of guardrails at request time.

[07:32] Priya: Short answer: we have request-level controls for filters, and you can enforce prompt pre-processing via the console or a middleware. Anthropic's constitutional approach is different but functionally you can get equivalent safety modes; we also integrate with custom token filters if you need deterministic removal.

[08:45] Marta: latency — can you run us through typical latencies for hosted vs dedicated GPUs? We mostly need sub-400 p95 for 2k tokens.

[09:02] Priya: For hosted low-latency endpoints we see p95 for 2k tokens in the 250–450ms range depending on model family; dedicated gives a tighter tail — often sub-300ms p95 if you reserve the instance type and enable local KV cache. There's also a tradeoff with batching; if you batch aggressively you lower cost but can inflate latency for tail requests.

[10:20] Jordan: To quantify — we've got a sample cost calc in the parity sheet comparing per-token cost across OpenAI/Anthropic/Together vs Redwood with standard and quantized profiles; for your volume (you mentioned ~50M tokens/mo) switching to a 4-bit quantized serving profile plus caching typically reduces per-token CPU/GPU cost by 30–45%.

[11:45] Ellen: That sounds promising. When you say quantized profiles, do we need model conversion work or is that handled?

[12:03] Priya: Redwood handles the quantized runtime and we provide recommended model variants. For private deployments we can ship quantized weights or recommend a compatible open checkpoint; for hosted we maintain the variants and handle updates. Some minor revalidation of outputs is always recommended.

[13:30] Jordan: I'm going to paste the parity link here — note: this is redwood-managed doc: https://redwood.co/links/stormbridge-parity-2026 (link is demo placeholder)

[14:05] Samir: Thanks. Can we talk about embeddings/semantic search? We currently use OpenAI embeddings for recall and rerank with FAISS.

[14:22] Priya: Yes. Redwood exposes a embeddings endpoint with the same call pattern. The key differences: we version embeddings and surface batch embeddings and incremental upserts to your vector DB. We also show tokenization and dimensionality mapping in the sheet — some OpenAI models have 1536 dims and if you move to a Redwood-verified model there may be 1024 — we provide mapping and recommended retrain steps.

[16:12] Marta: How invasive is the code change? Our backend is Node/Express and we have a small adapter layer now.

[16:28] Jordan: In most cases it's just swapping the endpoint and adjusting a couple of parameter names. The parity doc includes a smoke-test repo with <200 lines change for our typical Node adapter. We'll share that.

[17:40] Priya: Now I'll run a quick live request so you can see streaming and function call parity. (typing sounds) 

[18:05] Priya: Sending a sample chat -> Redwood API, streaming enabled. You'll see chunked tokens appear in the Console here. (pause) The Console also shows token breakdown and cost per call, which is handy for debugging unexpected prompts.

[20:01] Samir: I see that. There's a small difference in how Together streams chunk boundaries — sometimes the assistant name is on a separate event — but we can normalize client-side.

[21:20] Priya: Correct. We added small compatibility flags in the SDK to normalize events if you want an identical client surface.

[22:14] Jordan: Let's surface some obs on edge cases — long-running tool chains, RLHF style feedback loops, and prompt caches. For long contexts we recommend prefix caching and a dynamic KV cache to avoid re-encoding the system prompt for each request. That gives big perf wins for multi-step flows.

[24:01] Marta: Can the KV cache be shared across models or is it model-specific? We run multimodel ensembles occasionally.

[24:18] Priya: Cache is keyed by model variant and prompt shape — you can configure cross-model TTLs but by default it's model-specific. For ensembles we suggest warming the cache on dedicated infra during rollout.

[26:00] Speaker 2 (misattributed): There's also a question about telemetry privacy — do you keep transcripts?

[26:15] Jordan: For hosted API, we retain minimal logs for billing and troubleshooting; customers can opt-out and choose private deployment to keep everything in their VPC. We also support custom retention policies and log redaction.

[27:40] Ellen: For Private, what's the deployment pattern — do you give an appliance or a Helm chart? Our infra team prefers K8s with strict network egress control.

[28:02] Priya: We support a few patterns: 1) VPC-based private control plane with dedicated nodes in your cloud subscription, 2) on-prem zip deploy with an air-gapped package, or 3) a Helm chart for k8s with an operator for lifecycle. All have KMS/HSM integration options. We'll scope exact network requirements in the security call.

[30:10] Samir: Any gotchas around model licensing when migrating weights from Together/open checkpoints?

[30:35] Priya: Yes licensing matters — for open checkpoints we make sure you comply with the model license; for Together model variants we can run an interoperability layer if direct weights aren't transferrable. We'll list specifics in the parity doc per-model.

[32:00] Jordan: Quick pause to show Redwood Optimize — the Optimize tab suggests batching thresholds, quantization profile, and cache TTL based on observed traffic. For example, it recommended a 40ms batching window to hit your 50M tokens/month target while keeping p95 under 400ms.

[33:42] Marta: How do you measure quality regressions if we change quantization or model? We can't afford a drop in NPS.

[34:05] Priya: We tie quality monitors to prompt sets and evals. Optimize stores baseline evals and re-runs them on new model variants; if a regression crosses a threshold you get an alert. You can set human review gates before promotion.

[35:30] Samir: Would you help run a blind A/B comparing OpenAI vs Redwood outputs? We want a human-quality check.

[35:52] Jordan: Absolutely. That's part of the pilot: we'll run an A/B across your core prompts and bundle human review scaffolding. That pairs with our PRS (prompt regression suite) so regressions are quantified.

[37:00] Ellen: Network profile — do you support private endpoints over private link? Our security team will only allow PrivateLink style connections.

[37:25] Priya: We support AWS PrivateLink and equivalent cloud private link technologies, plus VPC peering if needed. We'll confirm details in the scoping call.

[38:40] Speaker 3 (Jordan): There's a question in chat about how Redwood handles backpressure when GPU is saturated. Priya, want to take that?

[38:50] Priya: Sure — Redwood runtime uses admission control and dynamic routing: requests can be routed to fallback smaller models or queued with a short TTL. For Dedicated customers we offer burst capacity pools so you don't see hard failures; failing over to a lower-cost model is also an option to preserve availability.

[40:05] Samir: For our SLA we prefer graceful degradation rather than high error rates. Can you set routes that prefer latency over cost?

[40:20] Priya: Yes, routing policies are policy-as-config. You can set priorities: latency-first, cost-first, region-first. The Console shows simulated decision traces so you can validate expected routing.

[42:00] Jordan: Ok, demo wrap-up — we've shown API parity examples, streaming & function calling, embeddings mapping, and Optimize suggestions. I'll read out the agreed pilot scope: 1) Parity spreadsheet review and code smoke test, 2) 1-week perf pilot (10k req/day synthetic) measuring p95 and cost, 3) security scoping call for Private/VPC options.

[43:05] Marta: That aligns. Couple of practical questions — pricing: do you have an enterprise discount model or committed capacity plan?

[43:20] Jordan: Yes: hosted is usage-based with volume tiers; Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commits. For your scale we can propose a blended committed rate; the parity spreadsheet will include a sample blended model vs pay-as-you-go.

[44:30] Ellen: For procurement, we will need SOC 2, ISO docs, MPLA/contract templates, and contact for legal.

[44:46] Jordan: I will attach our security pack (SOC2, ISO certs) and a standard SOW + contract template in the follow-up email. Legal contact will be cc'd.

[46:00] Samir: For the pilot, is there an SDK we should use or do we call REST directly?

[46:12] Priya: We have SDKs for Node, Python, and Java. The SDKs include helper adapters for streaming normalization and function-calling compatibility flags. For the pilot we typically recommend SDK usage for ease.

[47:35] Jordan: Quick live note — if you look at the Console trace I just opened, it shows token-level cost and a small sanity check saying the call used 318 tokens and estimated $0.0017. Those numbers will vary by model but it's good for cost debugging.

[48:58] Marta: Great to see the transparency. One more: retention of fine-tuning or private model weights — how does Redwood handle customer-owned fine-tune artifacts?

[49:20] Priya: For Private you can store weights in your S3 or on-prem artifact store and we can point runtime to them. For hosted we support private model uploads tied to your org and we provide encryption-at-rest. There's more detail in the security pack.

[51:00] Jordan: Alright, let's capture explicit next steps in the call. I'll read them and we can adjust: 1) Share parity + cost spreadsheet (Jordan) 2) Priya runs the perf pilot (redwood) 3) Ellen shares security contacts and network requirements (Stormbridge) 4) Schedule security scoping call for week of 7/27. Any changes?

[51:22] Marta: Sounds right. Add legal/doc packet to step 1.

[51:30] Jordan: Will do.

[52:00] Samir: One nit — sometimes transcriptions mention "KV cache" as K V cache, that can be confusing. Make sure the parity doc clarifies terminology.

[52:12] Priya: Good note, we'll normalize terms: KV cache, prefix cache, etc.

[53:30] Jordan: Any other questions from the team?

[53:40] Ellen: Not right now. We'll digest and come back with network diagrams.

[54:00] Marta: Thanks, this was helpful.

[54:08] Jordan: Great. We'll follow up with the parity sheet and the links to the quickstart repo and security pack. Expect an email by EOD tomorrow.

[55:03] (brief side conversation, low volume)

[56:20] Priya: One last quick note — for the benchmark we'll include both hosted and dedicated configs so you can see the tradeoffs. Also we'll include a small A/B script you can run to collect human review labels.

[58:05] Jordan: Perfect, thank you all. We'll close the recording.

[58:12] (meeting ends, a couple of after-call comments)

Post-call notes (auto):
